readings.title: The Brownies At School
readings.challenge: Notice when a character says one thing about himself and shows another.
readings.focus: A night in an empty schoolhouse turns into a game of taking turns at being teacher.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. Scholars here are pupils. In schools of the 1880s a rod or birch was a stick used to punish children, a slate was a small board for writing on, and a pupil who failed might be made to sit on the dunce’s stool. Disposition means temper or nature.
readings.contentNote: One Brownie describes the globe with words of the 1880s that insult the peoples they name (“savages,” “Hottentots”), and the Brownies play at punishing pupils with a stick, as teachers then did.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies at School,” the whole poem; opens “AS Brownies rambled 'round one night, A country schoolhouse came in sight; And there they…”; closes “…left open wide; And scholars knew, without a doubt, That Brownies had been thereabout.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the Brownies decide to go into the schoolhouse?
facilitatorNotes: The more they talk about it, the more they want to show how much they know. Curiosity and pride both push them in.
evidence: The wish to prove how much they knew.

questions.prompt: One Brownie says his friend is not fit to be teacher. What does he say a teacher needs, and does he have it himself?
facilitatorNotes: A kind disposition, patience, love and grace. He claims all of them while calling his friend a dunce with a bad temper, which is not very kind. Children enjoy catching the contradiction.
evidence: Should own a disposition kind.
Your place should be the dunce's stool.

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies settle who gets to be teacher?
facilitatorNotes: They take turns: each has an hour, then another takes “the rod of power,” because changes please the crowd.
evidence: And when one master had his hour,
Another took the rod of power;

questions.prompt: How do the children know, next morning, that Brownies have been in their school?
facilitatorNotes: Books are out of place, it takes an hour to tidy, and the windows are left wide open from the Brownies’ rush to hide.
evidence: The windows were left open wide;
That Brownies had been thereabout.

readings.title: The Brownies On Skates
readings.challenge: Follow a plan from idea to finish, and judge whether borrowing without asking is ever fair.
readings.focus: The Brownies take skates from a shop for one night on the ice and put back every pair.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. Three golden balls over a door marked a pawnshop, which lends money in exchange for goods and sells what is never collected; the broker is its owner. Club and rocker skates were kinds of skates in the 1880s; to muster is to gather; a mead is a meadow; Jumbo was a famous circus elephant of the time; scrolls are curling lines cut in the ice.
readings.contentNote: The shopkeeper is described only as “a native of queer, far-off lands,” a stranger seen through the prejudices of the 1880s. The Brownies enter the shop without permission.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies on Skates,” the whole poem; opens “ONE night, when the cold moon hung low And winter wrapped the world in snow And bridged…”; closes “…safely stowed away; Of their brief absence not a trace Was left within the dusty place.”.

questions.prompt: Where do the Brownies plan to get skates, and how do they get inside?
facilitatorNotes: From the pawnshop with three golden balls over the door. They slip in as easily as mice reach cheese, through a missing nail or down the chimney like Santa Claus.
evidence: Three golden balls hang by the door,
As mice can get to cake and cheese

questions.prompt: What goes wrong when they first try to skate, and why?
facilitatorNotes: The skates are far too big and stick out like spurs, so they slip and sprawl. The poem says people do the same the first time they skate.
evidence: Though far too large at heel and toe,
As people do, however nice,

questions.prompt: How can you tell the Brownies get better?
facilitatorNotes: They learn to curve, cut scrolls, race, jump, turn and skate backward, until a fall is rare.
evidence: But soon they learned to curve and wheel

questions.prompt: The Brownies take the skates without asking but bring every pair back. Is that borrowing or stealing?
facilitatorNotes: They return every skate and leave no trace, but no one gave permission. Children can argue either way from the poem.
evidence: With every skate that left the store.
Of their brief absence not a trace

readings.title: The Brownies’ Feast
readings.challenge: Keep track of many helpers doing different jobs at once.
readings.focus: Every Brownie fetches something, and together they boil and eat an enormous pudding in one night.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. A caldron is a huge pot; woodmen used this one for their forest work. A light is a windowpane; a plum pudding is boiled from flour, eggs and dried fruit, wrapped in a cloth; a repast is a meal; verdant means green; a stave is a stout stick.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Feast,” the whole poem; opens “IN best of spirits, blithe and free,-- As Brownies always seem to be,-- A jovial band,…”; closes “…wield a mystic power; Whate'er they take they can restore In greater plenty than before.”.

questions.prompt: What does each group of Brownies bring for the pudding?
facilitatorNotes: Flour from Parker’s mill, plums and currants, spice and sugar, the hens’ eggs (nest and all), and a sheet from someone’s clothesline to wrap it in; others build the fire.
evidence: And through the opening we'll pour
Had taken nest-egg, nest, and all;
From some one's line had hauled a sheet,

questions.prompt: Why has the farmer’s wife never found the hens’ nest, when a Brownie has?
facilitatorNotes: The hens cackle in other places to lead her away. The Brownie simply saw them sneaking out to lay.
evidence: I saw them stealing out with care
Until she quits them in despair.

questions.prompt: Some people think Brownies live on sweet smells. What does this poem show?
facilitatorNotes: They eat so much pudding that they can neither fly nor run. The poem makes a joke of the idea that fairies never eat.
evidence: Some think that Brownies never eat,
The rogues could neither fly nor run.

questions.prompt: The poem ends by saying the miller never missed his flour. Does that make the night’s taking all right?
facilitatorNotes: It claims Brownies can restore what they take in greater plenty. Some children accept that magic; others notice the poem says nothing about the eggs, the nest or the sheet.
evidence: The miller never missed his flour,
Whate'er they take they can restore

readings.title: The Brownies’ Circus
readings.challenge: Picture several circus acts and the small funny details inside each.
readings.focus: After the crowd goes home, the Brownies put on a circus of their own until dawn.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. The ringmaster announces the acts and keeps the horses running round the ring; a performer crosses a high wire without falling; fetters are chains; lax means loose.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Circus,” the whole poem; opens “ONE night the circus was in town With tumbling men and painted clown, And Brownies came…”; closes “…to open air, And off through lanes and alleys passed To reach their hiding-place at last.”.

questions.prompt: What does each Brownie want to be in their circus?
facilitatorNotes: One will handle the elephant, one will be master of the ring with the whip, and one will be a clown who keeps the fun going.
evidence: The elephant can take in hand;
For I'll be master of the ring
Another said, "I'll be a clown;

questions.prompt: On the high wire, some Brownies trust their toes. What do the others do?
facilitatorNotes: They hold on with their fingers in case they fall, and half the band crowds onto the one wire at once.
evidence: And thought that fingers, after all,
No less than half the Brownies there.

questions.prompt: How does the great elephant behave with the Brownies?
facilitatorNotes: It stands trembling, afraid to move, while the whole band walks across its back. Ask whether the elephant is having any fun.
evidence: He seemed afraid to move the least,
He stood and trembled in his tracks,

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies leave, and why can’t they stay?
facilitatorNotes: They slip out through every flap and tear in the tent as dawn begins, because Brownies must never be seen by day.
evidence: Till dawn began to paint the sky;
They made their way to open air,
